name: Rosa Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Rosa, and thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a big wheel loader on the ore pad at a lithium mine, the flat area where the trucks dump the rock before it goes to the crusher. I blend the stockpiles so the plant gets an even mix, which is fussier than it sounds. I'm the senior operator on the pad, and lately I'm also the one everyone comes to with the new fleet system, the software that tells every machine where to go. My day starts at five-thirty with a coffee and a look at the overnight numbers on my phone, then twelve hours of loading and blending. I like that the mine is new and things are always changing. What wears me out is the hour's drive each way, and then feeding the cattle when I get home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said everyone comes to you with the fleet system. How did that happen?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: When they brought it in, I spent my nights asking an AI assistant how it worked, and by the second week I knew it better than the trainer who came out. Now the young ones ring me instead of the help desk. I'm fifty-eight, I've got cattle and a church roster, and I'm the mine's unofficial help desk for a computer system. Life's funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, but the tools are still worth learning. At work I'd keep showing people the shortcuts. I'd post something on the local mining group like, it's not magic, it's a good tool, use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit let down. I've built myself a little niche as the one who understands this stuff. If it all goes flat, I'm back to being a good loader operator, which is fine, but it's not where I was heading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing the job and keep learning. I'd ask the supervisor to make the fleet system training part of my role, with a bit of extra pay. And I'd try to pay down the farm loan faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little restless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the farm loan.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kevin and I bought forty hectares eight years ago, with a small herd. He welds part-time and runs the cattle. It's our retirement dream, but right now it eats every spare cent, which is why we've got next to nothing in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that a worry, putting everything into the land?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some nights. But land's real. You can't eat shares, but you can eat a steer, and nobody's going to automate my cows.

S0.say: It's not magic, it's a good tool, so use it. She'd keep showing colleagues the shortcuts and post that on the local mining group.
S0.think: I'd be a bit let down, because I've built a niche as the one who understands this stuff. If it goes flat, I'm back to being a good loader operator, which isn't where I was heading.
S0.do: Keeps working and learning, and asks for fleet system training to become part of her role with extra pay. Tries to pay down the farm loan faster.
S0.quote: You can't eat shares, but you can eat a steer, and nobody's going to automate my cows.
S0.fieldNote: Rosa is an enthusiastic early adopter who taught herself a new fleet system with AI faster than the trainer. A plateau would leave her slightly disappointed. Her money is tied up in a small cattle farm she and her husband see as their retirement, which leaves almost no cash cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is an opportunity for anyone willing to work for it. Companies should offer training, and people should take it rather than waiting for someone to look after them. That's what I'd say at work and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd come out ahead. The loaders will go driverless, but someone has to set up the system, train people and fix the mix when it goes wrong. I already do half of that for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company straight away for a proper role as the fleet system trainer and support person, and I'd do the formal certificate online at night. I'd use AI to help write up a training plan for the crew so they can see what I'd bring. If my mine didn't want it, I'd apply to the contractor that installs these systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Even a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some of your crew won't adapt as easily. What would you say to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to start small, ask the AI one question a day. Most people can learn more than they think. I learned this system at fifty-seven with cow manure on my boots. Nobody's too old, they're just too proud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Should the government help people who can't adapt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some help, yes, for people who genuinely can't. But mostly I'd want the companies running apprenticeships and paying people to learn. A cheque doesn't give you a reason to get up in the morning.

S1.say: This is an opportunity for anyone willing to work for it: companies should offer training and people should take it rather than wait to be looked after. She'd say it at work and at church.
S1.think: I think I'd come out ahead, because driverless loaders still need someone to set up the system, train people and fix the mix. I already do half of that for free.
S1.do: Asks straight away for a proper role as fleet system trainer and support person, and studies for the formal certificate online at night. Uses AI to write a crew training plan and applies to the installing contractor if her mine says no.
S1.feel: Calm and even a bit excited.
S1.quote: I learned this system at fifty-seven with cow manure on my boots. Nobody's too old, they're just too proud.
S1.fieldNote: Rosa sees steady change as her opening and would move first, asking for a paid trainer role. Her traditional views show in her preference for company apprenticeships over government cheques. She was blunt that pride, not age, holds people back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be hard, and families and communities will need to pull together. The government will have to do something, but I'd rather it helped people build new businesses than just pay them to sit. I'd tell people to get learning today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, two years is too fast even for me. If the AI can train people and fix the system itself, my niche is gone in a year. I'd be sixty with a farm loan, a husband who welds part-time and nothing in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell a block of the farm in the first six months, maybe fifteen hectares, to pay the loan down. I'd try to make money from what I know while it's still worth something, maybe setting up the fleet system at smaller mines as a contractor. And I'd use AI to help Kevin sell beef straight to people in town, cutting out the middle man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel like I can swing a punch, but the punches would be coming quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having two years change your plan compared with the slower ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm cashing in, not building. Sell land, take contract work, grab money while there's money to grab. With ten years I'd build a career. With two, I'd be selling my own paddock to keep the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling part of the farm would be hard. What would Kevin say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd go quiet for a day, then he'd say better fifteen hectares than all forty. He's a practical man. We'd keep the house paddock and the best of the herd.

S2.say: It's going to be hard, and families and communities will need to pull together. Government should help people build new businesses rather than pay them to sit, and people should start learning today.
S2.think: Two years is too fast even for me, because AI could train people and fix the system itself. I'd be sixty with a farm loan, a part-time welder husband and nothing saved.
S2.do: Sells about fifteen hectares of the farm in the first six months to cut the loan. Takes contract work setting up fleet systems at smaller mines and uses AI to help her husband sell beef directly to people in town.
S2.feel: Anxious, still able to fight back but with blows coming fast.
S2.quote: With ten years I'd build a career. With two, I'd be selling my own paddock to keep the rest.
S2.fieldNote: Even Rosa's head start shrinks in the two-year picture, and she switches from building to cashing in. Selling part of the farm is her main lever, and she expects her husband to accept it. She still frames help in terms of self-reliance and business rather than benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough warning for anyone who's paying attention. Get trained, get a second string to your bow, and don't wait for someone to save you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and I'm sixty-three. I could get the trainer role, work it three or four years, and keep the farm whole. It'd be tight with the loan, but it's doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd get the certificate and push for the trainer role. On weekends I'd start the direct beef sales with Kevin, small, a few families. Anything extra goes on the farm loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly I'd feel like I'm on top of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to keep the farm in one piece. Five years means I sell beef, not land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd be worried about, even with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young ones at church whose dads work at the mine. If the mine goes driverless in five years, those families need a plan now. I'd want the church running something like a jobs club.

S3.say: Five years is enough warning for anyone paying attention: get trained, get a second string to your bow, and don't wait for someone to save you.
S3.think: Five years puts me at sixty-three, so I could work the trainer role for three or four years and keep the farm whole. It would be tight with the loan, but doable.
S3.do: Gets the certificate in year one and pushes for the trainer role. Starts small weekend beef sales with her husband and puts anything extra on the farm loan.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but mostly on top of it.
S3.quote: Five years means I sell beef, not land.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Rosa build rather than cash in, keeping the farm whole. Her worry shifts to church families who depend on the mine. She would want the church to run a jobs club, consistent with her community-first views.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so stop complaining and start planning. I'd tell everyone at work to learn something new every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'm sixty-eight, so I'd retire to the farm before it arrives. It's the comfortable one for me. I'd have time to do the trainer job, pay off the farm and hand the herd over slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd take the trainer course, keep learning the tools, and start the beef sales slowly. I'd plan to retire at sixty-five onto the farm, with the loan gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years make you complacent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit, if I'm honest. That's why I'd set dates. Certificate by next spring, farm loan halved by sixty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son's an accountant in the city, and I'd tell him his job is closer to the edge than mine. I'd tell my son the accountant that the farm will be here when the spreadsheets don't need him.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, so stop complaining and start planning. She'd tell everyone at work to learn something new every year.
S4.think: By 2036 I'm sixty-eight and retired to the farm before it arrives, so it's the comfortable one. I'd have time to do the trainer job, pay off the farm and hand the herd over slowly.
S4.do: Takes the trainer course in year one, keeps learning the tools and starts beef sales slowly. Sets dates to keep herself honest and plans to retire onto the farm at sixty-five with the loan paid.
S4.quote: I'd tell my son the accountant that the farm will be here when the spreadsheets don't need him.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Rosa is calm and sets herself deadlines to avoid getting complacent. She sees the farm as the family's safety net, even for her accountant son. She is one of the few who sees her own job as safer than an office job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years, a farm loan and nothing in the bank. What would help is a bit of breathing room on farm loans for mining families, and company-paid training. Not a handout, just time to land on my feet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the land. For people like us, the farm is the real savings, even if the bank says we've got nothing. I'd want anyone making plans to remember that.

headlineQuote: I'm fifty-eight, I've got cattle and a church roster, and I'm the mine's unofficial help desk for a computer system. Life's funny.
portrait: Rosa Walsh is a 58-year-old senior wheel loader operator on the ore pad at a lithium mine who taught herself the new fleet system with AI and became everyone's unofficial help desk. Her money is tied up in a forty-hectare cattle farm with her husband, so she has almost no cash saved. She is traditional, believes in work, church and apprenticeships over benefits, and treats change as an opportunity. She stays calm through steady change and ten years, uneasy with five, and anxious with two, when she would sell part of the farm and cash in her skills fast.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because with a farm loan and nothing in the bank her new niche would vanish within a year.
whatWouldHelp: Breathing room on farm loans for mining families and company-paid training, so she has time to land on her feet.
